A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work, renamed from BiLB4MTL to LDC-MTL. Their main texts, figures, tables, equations and complete appendices support reliable matching and comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original experiments on a synthetic example and four MTL benchmarks, including accuracy, runtime and normalization-ablation results.

after.justification: V2 retains original benchmark experiments and adds loss/gradient diagnostics, sensitivity tests, component ablations and task-order experiments.

M1.justification: The bilevel objectives, penalty formulation and updates in Algorithms 1–2 remain unchanged. V1's 'identical normalization' becomes 'no normalization' in v2 Appendix A.1; this and the method renaming do not establish a procedural change.

E1.justification: Both evaluate the same synthetic two-task example, CelebA's 40 attributes, QM9's 11 properties, Cityscapes' two tasks and NYU-v2's three tasks. Added diagnostics and controls retain these datasets and task requirements.

E2.justification: The main benchmark comparator rosters are unchanged; MoCo already appears in v1 Tables 1 and 4. V2 adds LS to the QM9 loss-trajectory comparison (v1 Figure 3 versus v2 Figure 6) and to new loss/gradient diagnostics. Weight sweeping further evaluates the existing LS method.

E3.justification: V2 substantially expands the evaluation design with LS-weight and penalty sweeps, normalization-by-LDC component controls, shuffled-loss testing and gradient comparisons on eight sampled CelebA tasks after epoch 15. Core splits and training budgets remain. The reported Δm sign convention is corrected. V2 Table 6 lists NYU-v2's step size as 8e-5, whereas both setup passages state 1e-4; this does not establish a rerun.

E4.justification: V1's detailed normalization-alternative grid is replaced by normalization/LDC component ablations on QM9 and NYU-v2. V2 additionally investigates penalty sensitivity, loss ordering, loss distributions, gradient conflicts, weight trajectories and trade-offs against weight-swept LS. The existing small-gradient diagnostic is retained and relocated.

E5.justification: Both versions report three-run averages. V2 newly supplies standard deviations for the proposed method's aggregate results across all four benchmarks and for several additional controls (Tables 6–11), without reporting an increased run count. Most baseline and task-specific results remain mean-only.

E6.justification: Retained best Δm scores remain unchanged: Cityscapes -0.57, CelebA -1.31, QM9 49.5 and NYU-v2 -4.40. V2 adds substantial diagnostic and controlled-experiment results, including CelebA loss means of 0.1888 versus LS's 0.2872 and task-reordering results of -1.28 versus -1.31. Alternative-τ rows and the old normalization grid are removed, including QM9's τ=1 result of 113.6.

T1.justification: The main convergence framework and proofs remain, including the O(epsilon^-2) rate in Appendix C despite its removal from theorem statements. Local edits correct the Δm sign definition, explicitly use the lower-level gradient in the PL assumption and change T=Omega(epsilon^-2) to T=O(epsilon^-2). V2 also introduces an inconsistent Phi=gradient(f)+lambda gradient(g) expression where v1 used Phi=f+lambda g.

C1.justification: The core bilevel formulation, computational-complexity, convergence and benchmark-performance claims persist. V2 extends the introduction's contributions with claims about reduced gradient conflict, superiority to weight-swept LS and the importance of dynamic training trajectories.

C2.justification: V2 substantially expands the mechanism discussion: losses need not become equal, changing training trajectories matters despite nearly uniform final weights, LS can favor easier tasks, and comparable loss scales may explain insensitivity to task ordering. V1's discussion of poor QM9 performance with τ=1 disappears alongside that result.

D1.justification: V2 newly identifies one NVIDIA A6000 GPU, describes the router's shared-feature input and tabulates selected step sizes, penalty constants and τ choices for each dataset. V1's explicit coarse-to-fine grid-search recipe is omitted. These are documentation changes; the PDFs do not establish corresponding implementation changes.

R1.justification: V2 adds engagement with Kurin et al. and Xin et al. concerning strong scalarization baselines, plus citations to Bayesian gradient aggregation, gap balancing and the evaluation metric. It removes the generalized-smoothness discussion and citation to Qi Zhang et al. The broader MTL/bilevel positioning remains.

P1.justification: Beyond renaming the title and method, v2 rewrites the introduction around loss discrepancy, reorganizes Section 5 into results and analysis, moves experimental setup into Appendix A.1 and substantially restructures Appendix A. Terminology changes throughout, and the impact statement is removed.

P2.justification: V2 adds loss-distribution plots, gradient heatmaps, trade-off scatter plots, weight trajectories and several analysis tables. Earlier loss/gradient figures move to the appendix, with an LS panel added to the loss plot. Main benchmark tables are consolidated, detailed QM9 results move to the appendix, and algorithms receive new boxed layouts.

improvement.justification: Weight-swept LS controls, component/order/sensitivity tests, standard deviations and selected hyperparameters strengthen the empirical support and reproducibility of the retained findings. The gain is tempered by removed alternative-τ and normalization comparisons and new inconsistencies: NYU-v2's learning rate and normalization labels disagree across Appendix A.1 and Tables 5–6, while Appendix C inconsistently redefines Phi. Overall, the added evidence provides a limited net quality improvement.
